newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebel Zaire leader vows march on Mobutu's hometown.
newsitem.headline: Rebel Zaire leader vows march on Mobutu's hometown.

text.p: The leader of east Zaire's rebels told supporters on Thursday his forces would march on to the distant hometown of President Mobutu Sese Seko.

"You had 35 years of dictatorship and there has been no development in the country because of Mobutu. We are going to push on towards Gbadolite. Are you ready?" Laurent Kabila asked a crowd of some 5,000 people in the eastern town of Bukavu.
"We've been ready for a long time," some shouted back.
But when Mobutu's long-time opponent informed the crowd he would open a military recruitment office in Bukavu the next day, the response was some muted grumbling rather than cheers.
The people of the town on the border with Rwanda, one of the first the rebels seized in a three-week-old offensive that has plunged Zaire into turmoil, seemed tired of war.

Kabila, a comrade-in-arms in the 1960s of Marxist guerrilla Che Guevara, promised the relaxed crowd of civilians outside war-scarred Bukavu's post office the rebels would soon restore electricity, free movement and bring in a new currency.
Peace has returned to the lakeside town, a one-time holiday resort, but no one can move out to areas where the rebels are believed still to be fighting ill-disciplined Zairean troops.
Zairean banknotes, bearing the face of Mobutu, lay in the streets, ignored and worthless on this side of the front line.
Exhausted refugees from Bukavu have started arriving in Kisangani more than 500 km (300 miles) northwest on the other side of the lines and less than halfway to Mobutu's remote hometown, Gbadolite.
Mobutu, president since 1965 and now in France after treatment for cancer in Switzerland, has not been in Zaire for months.
Kabila, 56, says he leads the Alliance of Democratic Forces for Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), whose cutting edge is the force of ethnic Tutsis now controlling much of the east.
"The aim of the alliance is to put an end to Mobutu's autocratic rule and to banish his corruption from Zaire," Kabila told Reuters in October. He says now Bukavu will be his base.
From mineral-rich southern Zaire, he is not a Tutsi. He has opposed Mobutu since a 1960s rebellion just after independence.
